title: Give a Dog a Good Name

chapterBreakdown.gentle: People often respond to the name attached to them. Carnegie uses a good reputation because a believable identity can guide behavior upward. The chapter keeps one limit clear. The good name has to feel credible, not fake or magical.
chapterBreakdown.direct: The chapter treats reputation as a behavioral scaffold. A person may try to live up to an offered identity if it feels real enough to inhabit. The move fails when the label is empty branding or manipulation.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: A believable name can pull behavior upward. The identity has to be real enough to wear. Fake labels kill the effect.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: People do not respond only to rules or corrections. They also respond to the kind of person they believe they are becoming. Carnegie therefore turns to giving someone a good name. The chapter is not mystical about this. It treats reputation as a scaffold. When a person is offered a believable identity such as careful, reliable, or capable, they may begin to act in ways that fit it. That is especially useful when progress is already beginning and needs a more stable frame. The chapter also keeps its limit clear. A good name cannot be an empty slogan pasted over reality. If the label feels fake, manipulative, or socially performative, it loses force quickly. So the move works only when the reputation points toward something credible that the person can plausibly inhabit. Then the name stops being costume language and becomes a behavioral standard the person may try to honor. That prepares the way for Chapter 29, where the book turns from identity support to making faults feel easier to correct.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Carnegie treats a good reputation as a behavior-shaping offer. People often try to live up to identities that feel available and believable. If someone is described as careful or dependable in a way that fits reality enough to be plausible, that description can influence later choices. In that sense reputation becomes a scaffold for conduct rather than a decorative compliment. But the chapter is not naive about manipulation. A false label or theatrical branding move can feel hollow and may damage trust instead of helping. The offered identity has to connect to real capacity, real progress, or a credible direction of growth. When it does, the person may start organizing behavior around the name they have been given. This extends the prior chapter: small gains become more stable when they start to attach to a self-story.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: People often move toward the identity that the room makes believable for them. Carnegie uses a good name because a strong reputation can act like a rail for behavior. Call someone careful, reliable, or capable in a credible way and they may start playing toward that standard. That is the upside. The limit is just as important. If the name is fake, inflated, or detached from evidence, it turns into branding theater and loses power fast. The method works only when the label feels like a real lane the person could step into. Then reputation stops being fluff and starts shaping decisions. That is why the next chapter follows well. Once identity is pulling upward, faults can be framed as more correctable instead of more crushing.

chapterBreakdown.gentle: Behavior is shaped not only by rules and consequences but also by the identities people believe are open to them. Carnegie uses that fact by giving someone a good name. The chapter does not treat reputation as magic. It treats it as a believable identity offer that can alter what kinds of choices feel fitting. When a person is described as careful, dependable, or capable in a way that plausibly connects to reality, that description can become a scaffold for future conduct. The person may begin to act toward the offered standard because the name starts to feel inhabitable. This is especially powerful when improvement has already begun and needs a more durable frame than isolated praise. But the method depends on credibility. If the label is inflated, dishonest, or socially theatrical, it stops functioning as scaffold and starts functioning as manipulation. The chapter therefore succeeds only when the reputation is concrete enough to be believable and generous enough to invite the person upward without denying reality.
chapterBreakdown.direct: Carnegie treats a good reputation as a way of shaping behavior through identity rather than through command alone. People often organize action around the kind of person they think they are or could plausibly become. A credible good name can exploit that tendency constructively. Once the identity offer lands, choices that fit the reputation may begin to feel more natural, expected, or self-respecting. That is the behavioral scaffold at the center of the chapter. The method also has a sharp limit. False labels, exaggerated branding, or theatrical praise can turn the move manipulative and break trust. The reputation must connect to actual capacity, visible progress, or a believable direction of growth. When it does, the name can stabilize conduct that earlier praise only began to encourage. In that sense the chapter turns momentum into identity support rather than leaving progress as a series of disconnected wins.
chapterBreakdown.competitive: People play toward the identity that the room makes believable. Carnegie uses a good name to bend that fact toward improvement. If you offer someone a credible reputation, the label can start acting like a rail that keeps choices moving in the same direction. That is the advantage. But the method has no power if the name is fake. Inflated branding, empty labels, or social theater can make the identity offer feel manipulative, and then the whole move collapses. The label has to sit close enough to the facts that the person can wear it without feeling lied to. When that happens, behavior often starts organizing itself around the better name. That is why the next chapter can move into easier correction. Once identity is pulling upward, faults do not have to feel like permanent verdicts.
